title: Vacuum, Fan & Small Household Appliance Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A mature, import-exposed US manufacturing niche where branded innovation in cleaning, cooking, air treatment and personal-care appliances is fighting weak housing demand, tariff volatility and offshore cost advantages.
overview: Operators manufacture small electric appliances and housewares including blenders, coffee makers, blow-dryers, portable heaters, portable air-treatment products, household fans and floor-care equipment such as vacuums, waxers and polishers. The industry excludes major appliances such as refrigerators, dishwashers, microwaves and air conditioners. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline placed revenue at $4.16 billion, down 0.5% in 2022, while the October 2024 IBISWorld update described revenue as falling at a 2.7% CAGR over the prior five years to $4.0 billion in 2023, including a 1.2% 2023 decline. The latest official Census AIES release reported 2023 NAICS 33521 employer-firm sales/value of shipments/revenue of $3.599 billion, annual payroll of $401.736 million and operating expenses of $2.237 billion. In 2025, demand is bifurcated: Circana reported US small appliance and housewares demand up 1% in the first five months of 2025, NIQ reported H1 2025 consumer tech and durables unit sales up 1% and dollar sales up 4.6%, and hygiene-related appliances including vacuum cleaners grew 6% in H1 2025, but manufacturers remain exposed to tariff costs, retailer inventory caution and weak home-purchase activity.

key_stats.market_size: 2023: $4.0 billion IBISWorld industry revenue estimate; 2023: $3.599 billion Census AIES NAICS 33521 employer-firm sales/value of shipments/revenue
key_stats.growth: 2018-2023: -2.7% revenue CAGR per October 2024 IBISWorld update; 2023: -1.2% estimated revenue decline
key_stats.businesses: 2025: 161 businesses, up 2.5% in 2025, per IBISWorld public statistics page
key_stats.official_payroll: 2023: $401.736 million annual payroll, Census AIES NAICS 33521
key_stats.official_operating_expenses: 2023: $2.237 billion operating expenses, Census AIES NAICS 33521
key_stats.retail_demand_signal: First five months of 2025: US small appliance and housewares demand up 1% year over year, Circana
key_stats.category_demand_signal: H1 2025: hygiene-related appliances including vacuum cleaners, washing machines and dishwashers grew 6% in sales, NIQ

baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022: small electric household appliances 56.6% of revenue, floor care equipment 18.7%, electric fans 15.6%, other 9.1%

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by designing, assembling or contracting production for branded and private-label small appliances sold through mass merchants, warehouse clubs, e-commerce marketplaces, department stores, grocery/drug channels, specialty electronics/appliance retailers and commercial distributors. Higher-margin revenue comes from differentiated products such as robotic and cordless vacuums, air purifiers, premium coffee/espresso machines, air fryers, multi-cookers, beauty appliances and connected home-environment devices; lower-margin volume comes from replacement and promotional countertop appliances, fans and basic floor-care units.
cost_structure: The cost base is dominated by purchased components, plastics/resins, metals, motors, electronics, packaging, freight, tariffs and retailer allowances. The 2022 baseline reported a 7.3% profit margin and $528.9 million in wages, while the Census AIES reported 2023 NAICS 33521 operating expenses of $2.237 billion and annual payroll of $401.736 million. 2025 company disclosures show tariff pressure was material: Newell Brands reported $174 million of 2025 gross cash tariff costs and Spectrum Brands cited 2025 tariffs, supply constraints and lower home-appliance volumes as headwinds. Automation, outsourced manufacturing and offshore sourcing remain central to cost control.
major_players: Newell Brands Inc. - IBISWorld identified Newell as the largest business in the industry in its 2025 public statistics page; Newell's Home & Commercial Solutions segment reported $3.772 billion of 2025 net sales, down 7.3% from 2024.

SharkNinja Inc. - US-based small appliance brand owner with 2025 total net sales of $6.399 billion, up 15.7% from 2024; 2025 cleaning appliances sales were $2.206 billion and food preparation appliances grew 31.6%.

Spectrum Brands Holdings - Home & Personal Care includes small home and personal-care appliances; fiscal Q4 2025 HPC net sales were $296.2 million, down 11.9% year over year, with home appliances down double digits.
iRobot Corp. - Roomba maker remained a key robotic vacuum brand but reported 2024 revenue down 23% and an operating loss of $103 million after the Amazon transaction was terminated in 2024.

BISSELL, Dyson, TTI/Hoover and other global branded suppliers - important competitors in US floor care and air-treatment categories, though much production is offshore or contract-manufactured rather than domestic NAICS manufacturing.
current_dynamics: The industry is balancing modest consumer demand with hard supply-side volatility. 2025 at-home consumption supported small appliances tied to cooking, cleaning, air quality and personal care, but replacement purchases remain price-sensitive. Imports remain the defining competitive constraint: the 2022 baseline put import penetration at 87.6% of domestic demand, and 2025 tariff changes raised landed-cost uncertainty for China-heavy supply chains. Retailers are pushing back on price increases and managing inventories carefully, while stronger brands are using innovation, advertising and distribution gains to offset weaker housing turnover.
whats_growing: 2025: air purifiers, vaporizers and home-comfort appliances grew double digits in Circana's first-five-months 2025 readout.
2025: hygiene-related appliances including vacuum cleaners grew 6% in H1 2025, according to NIQ.
2025: SharkNinja food preparation appliance sales grew 31.6% and beauty/home environment appliance sales grew 45.3% from 2024.
2025: Circana cited single-serve blenders, electric kettles, single-serve brewing systems, espresso makers, frothers, rice cookers, air fryers and slow cookers as leading growth categories.
2025: premium features such as robotics, cordless formats, self-emptying systems, air-quality sensing and multifunction cooking continue to lift average selling prices.
whats_shrinking: 2023: IBISWorld estimated industry revenue declined 1.2%, extending a 2.7% five-year CAGR decline to $4.0 billion.
2024: iRobot revenue declined 23% and the company reduced its global workforce by roughly 51% under restructuring actions.
2025: Spectrum Brands' fiscal Q4 Home & Personal Care net sales fell 11.9%, with home appliances down double digits.
2025: Newell Brands Home & Commercial Solutions net sales fell 7.3% from 2024 to $3.772 billion.
2025: low-end domestically made appliances continue to lose share to imported substitutes where price matters more than brand or features.
recent_developments: 2024-01-29: Amazon and iRobot terminated their planned $1.4 billion acquisition, and iRobot announced a restructuring that cut about 350 jobs, or 31% of its workforce.
2024-10-09: DOE finalized appliance certification and reporting changes, including provisions tied to air cleaners classified under NAICS 335210.
2025-10-15: NIQ reported H1 2025 consumer tech and durable-goods units up 1%, dollar sales up 4.6%, and hygiene-related appliance sales up 6%.
2026-02-06: Newell Brands reported 2025 net sales of $7.204 billion, Home & Commercial Solutions sales of $3.772 billion and $174 million of 2025 gross cash tariff costs.
2026-02-26: Census released final 2023 AIES manufacturing data showing NAICS 33521 sales/value of shipments/revenue of $3.599 billion.
2026-03-02: SharkNinja filed its 2025 10-K reporting $6.399 billion of 2025 net sales, up 15.7%, with US sales representing 62.5% of total net sales.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is cautiously mixed. Domestic manufacturing revenue should remain near the low-$4 billion range unless tariffs or reshoring incentives materially shift supply chains back to the US. Demand growth should come from premium cordless and robotic floor care, air purification, fans, compact cooking and beverage appliances, and beauty/home-environment devices, while commodity countertop appliances stay price-pressured. Manufacturers with strong brands, faster product cycles and tariff mitigation can gain share, but high import penetration, weak housing turnover, retailer bargaining power and cost inflation limit broad-based margin expansion.
themes: Import dependence and China tariff volatility
Premiumization in floor care, air treatment and cooking appliances
Robotics, cordless power and connected features
Retailer inventory discipline and price resistance
Mature domestic production base with selective automation
data_year: 2025 with 2026 source updates and 2023 latest official Census AIES manufacturing data
one_sentence: US vacuum, fan and small household appliance manufacturing remains a roughly $4 billion domestic industry, with 2025 demand helped by at-home living and hygiene categories but constrained by high import penetration, pressured consumers and volatile China-related tariffs.

title: Valve Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US valve manufacturers supply industrial, fluid-power and plumbing flow-control products into cyclical construction, energy, manufacturing and water-infrastructure markets.
overview: Operators manufacture metal valves, hose fittings, faucets, showerheads, trim and other flow-control devices used in industrial processes, hydraulic and pneumatic systems, plumbing, oil and gas, utilities, waterworks, refining, chemicals and construction. The 2022 baseline showed a post-pandemic rebound to $42.199 billion of revenue, but the April 2025 IBISWorld update estimated a smaller $38.8 billion market after weaker industrial production and rising import competition reduced demand for US-made standardized valves. The better-performing portion of the market is engineered and severe-service valves, where reliability, certification, automation and application expertise matter more than price.

key_stats.industrial_production: US manufacturing output was 1.1% above June 2025 levels in June 2026, while total industrial production was 1.1% higher year over year
key_stats.energy_end_market: US crude oil production reached a record 13.6 million barrels per day in 2025
key_stats.water_infrastructure: EPA reported $23 billion of WIFIA financing closed and $51 billion of water projects supported as of July 2026

baseline_2022.exports: $12.064 billion in 2022, equal to 28.6% of revenue
baseline_2022.imports: $19.799 billion in 2022, equal to 39.7% of domestic demand

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by selling industrial valves, fluid-power valves, hose fittings, plumbing fixture valves, trim and related flow-control components to OEMs, distributors, contractors, utilities and process-industry customers. Higher-margin sales come from engineered valves for oil and gas, refining, chemicals, power, water/wastewater, cryogenic, hydrogen and other severe-service applications, plus aftermarket parts, actuation, controls, calibration and repair support.
cost_structure: Costs are dominated by purchased materials and components, especially steel, iron, aluminum, brass, nonferrous alloys, castings, pipe and tube, elastomers, seals, actuators and electronics. Labor remains important for machining, assembly, testing, engineering and quality assurance, while other costs include energy, plant overhead, depreciation on machining and testing equipment, freight, warranty, certification, R&D and selling expenses. The 2025 tariff increase on steel and aluminum content raised input-cost risk for manufacturers and importers.
current_dynamics: In 2025, the industry was pressured by import penetration from lower-cost countries, weak pockets of industrial production and higher material-price exposure. In 2026, demand signals improved but remained uneven: the Federal Reserve reported June 2026 manufacturing output 1.1% above June 2025 and mining output 2.4% higher, supporting process, energy and heavy-industry valve demand, while construction-supply output declined 0.4% in June 2026. Energy remains a stabilizer because US crude production hit a 2025 record, but lower 2025 WTI prices and fewer rigs limited new upstream capital intensity. Water and wastewater infrastructure is a bright spot due to continuing EPA WIFIA and SRF funding, while tariffs and Buy America rules favor some domestic supply but complicate cost management.
whats_growing: Engineered industrial valves, severe-service process valves, automation-ready control valves, water and wastewater valves, utility transmission valves, cryogenic and hydrogen-related components, aftermarket service, and higher-spec products for energy, chemicals, power, pharmaceuticals and data-center-adjacent industrial infrastructure are growing faster than commodity plumbing trim.
whats_shrinking: Standardized plumbing fixture valves, commodity fittings and other price-sensitive products face continued pressure from imports and distributor private-label sourcing. Smaller domestic manufacturers with limited automation, certification breadth or engineering support are losing ground to larger consolidators and lower-cost foreign suppliers. Residential construction-linked demand is also less robust than public infrastructure and process-industry demand.
recent_developments: 2025-04: IBISWorld estimated US valve manufacturing revenue at $38.8 billion in 2025, down from the 2022 rebound peak.
2025-06-04: US Section 232 steel and aluminum tariffs increased from 25% to 50%, raising input-cost and sourcing risk for valve producers.
2025-09: VMA and the Hydraulic Institute held a 2025 Market Outlook Workshop focused on 2026 planning for oil and gas, construction, water/wastewater, chemicals, power and other end markets.
2025-11-20: EPA announced $6.5 billion of new WIFIA funding plus $550 million for states, supporting water and wastewater project pipelines that use industrial valves.
2026-03-31: EIA reported US crude oil production rose 3% in 2025 to a record 13.6 million barrels per day, supporting energy valve demand despite lower rig activity.
2026-07-17: Federal Reserve data showed June 2026 manufacturing output 1.1% above June 2025 and mining output 2.4% higher, pointing to firmer industrial end-market conditions.
outlook: Revenue is likely to grow modestly from the 2025 trough rather than return quickly to the 2022 spike. Tailwinds include public water investment, record US energy production, process-industry maintenance, automation and reshoring incentives. Headwinds include import competition, tariff-driven input volatility, uneven residential construction, lower oil-price sensitivity in upstream drilling and mature replacement cycles. The best-positioned manufacturers are those with engineered products, domestic qualification, automation, aftermarket channels and exposure to regulated infrastructure or mission-critical process markets.
themes: Buy America and domestic content rules
one_sentence: The industry remains mature and fragmented, with 2025 revenue below the 2022 rebound peak as low-cost imports, metal costs and uneven end-market demand offset stronger water infrastructure, process-industry, energy and specialized-valve opportunities.

title: Variable Message Signage Manufacturing
one_liner: U.S. manufacturers of programmable LED signs, digital billboards, scoreboards and transportation message displays are riding steady infrastructure and digital out-of-home demand, while component costs and tariffs keep margins tight.
overview: This industry manufactures electronic signs that display programmable text, graphics or video, including digital billboards, highway dynamic message signs, scoreboards, in-store displays and related control systems. The 2021 baseline positioned the industry as a low-concentration, low-import, growth-stage manufacturing market with revenue of $6.5 billion in 2021 and a projected path to about $7.1 billion by 2026. Current 2025-2026 conditions are mixed but constructive: U.S. out-of-home advertising hit a 2025 record, digital out-of-home kept gaining share, and federal highway programs under the IIJA continue to fund intelligent transportation systems and roadside safety infrastructure. At the same time, customers remain price-sensitive, display hardware is increasingly commoditized at the low end, and manufacturers face continuing exposure to LED modules, semiconductors, aluminum, steel, freight, labor and tariff volatility.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: about $7.0 billion in U.S. variable message signage manufacturing revenue, estimated from the 2021 IBISWorld baseline and its 2021-2026 revenue path.
key_stats.growth: 2025: about +1.7% industry revenue growth estimated for the narrow manufacturing industry; 2026: about $7.1 billion implied revenue.
key_stats.adjacent_us_digital_signage_market: 2025: $7.44 billion and 2026: $7.96 billion according to Grand View Research; Mordor Intelligence estimates 2025 at $9.07 billion and 2026 at $9.73 billion for broader U.S. digital signage systems.
key_stats.us_ooh_ad_revenue: 2025: $9.46 billion, up 3.6% year over year, according to OAAA.
key_stats.digital_ooh_share: 2025: digital out-of-home represented 36.3% of U.S. OOH revenue and grew 10.5% year over year, according to OAAA.
key_stats.baseline_profit_margin: 2021: 4.8% EBIT margin in the IBISWorld baseline; 2026 baseline projection was 4.9%.
key_stats.baseline_imports_exports: 2021: imports were $135.6 million and exports were $52.6 million; 2026 baseline projection was $146.1 million of imports and $57.9 million of exports.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: about $6.65 billion, estimated by applying the IBISWorld 2021-2026 projected CAGR to 2021 revenue of $6.538 billion.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: about +1.7% revenue growth, consistent with the baseline 2021-2026 projected CAGR.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2022: about 4.8%-4.9% EBIT margin implied by the baseline path.
baseline_2022.industry_position: 2022: growth-stage industry with low concentration, low globalization, medium competition and high revenue volatility.

how_it_makes_money.primary_revenue_streams: Manufacturers sell LED display cabinets, message centers, digital billboard faces, scoreboard/video-board systems, transportation dynamic message signs, control hardware, software and installation-related services.
how_it_makes_money.largest_product_area: 2021 baseline: digital billboards generated 65.4% of industry revenue.
how_it_makes_money.other_product_areas: 2021 baseline: scoreboards were 15.9%, transportation displays were 9.6%, in-store digital displays were 7.2%, and other digital signage was 1.9%.
how_it_makes_money.customer_groups: Outdoor advertising operators, media companies, retailers, restaurants, hotels, schools, colleges, stadiums, transit agencies, airports, departments of transportation and road contractors.
how_it_makes_money.pricing_model: Revenue is typically project-based, with higher margins on engineered systems, controls, software, warranty/service packages and custom integrations than on commoditized low-end LED displays.

cost_structure.2021_profit: IBISWorld baseline profit margin was 4.8% of revenue in 2021.
cost_structure.2021_wages: IBISWorld baseline wages were $2.267 billion in 2021, equal to roughly 34.7% of 2021 revenue.
cost_structure.major_input_costs: LED modules, semiconductors, printed circuit boards, power supplies, aluminum and steel cabinets, plastics/resins, glass/acrylic faces, wiring, freight, installation labor, software development and warranty service.
cost_structure.current_pressure_points: 2025-2026 cost risk is concentrated in imported electronic components, semiconductor availability, steel and aluminum prices, China-related tariffs and skilled technical labor.
cost_structure.margin_pattern: Margins are structurally modest because customers compare LED sign prices across many vendors, while public-sector contracts often emphasize bid compliance and lifecycle reliability.

current_dynamics.demand: 2025 demand is supported by record U.S. out-of-home advertising revenue, continued DOOH share gains, school and stadium scoreboard upgrades, and public-sector intelligent transportation spending.
current_dynamics.supply: Component supply is better than during the 2020-2022 shortage period, but manufacturers remain exposed to semiconductor, LED module, cabinet metal and power-electronics sourcing risk.
current_dynamics.competition: The low end is crowded with imported and private-label displays, while U.S. producers compete on brightness, weatherproofing, uptime, service response, controller software and compliance with transportation standards.
current_dynamics.technology: Pixel pitch keeps tightening, displays are brighter and more energy efficient, and vendors are adding cloud scheduling, remote monitoring, diagnostics, content automation and AI-assisted content tools.
current_dynamics.policy: IIJA highway funding through fiscal 2026 supports transportation display opportunities, while 2025 tariff increases on China-linked semiconductors and related strategic inputs raise procurement uncertainty.

whats_growing: 2025: Digital out-of-home advertising, with DOOH revenue up 10.5% and reaching 36.3% of U.S. OOH revenue.
2025: Transit OOH, which OAAA reported as the fastest-growing OOH segment for a second consecutive year, up 9.2%.
2025-2026: Highway, tolling, travel-time, lane-use and variable speed-limit displays tied to intelligent transportation systems.
2025-2026: School, high-school athletics, parks and recreation, and stadium video-board upgrades.
2026: Remote monitoring, cloud content management, lower-power LED cabinets and AI-assisted sign-content creation.
whats_shrinking: 2025-2026: Incandescent and older low-resolution message signs as LED replacements become standard.
2025-2026: Static sign share in locations where operators can monetize multiple digital messages from one face.
2025-2026: Low-end hardware margins as imported modules and commoditized indoor displays keep price competition intense.
2025-2026: Labor-intensive manual ad changeover demand where digital billboard networks replace vinyl rotations.
recent_developments: Jan. 1, 2025: USTR tariff increases took effect for selected China-linked strategic inputs, including a scheduled semiconductor tariff increase to 50%, raising electronics sourcing risk for display manufacturers.
June 3, 2025: OAAA reported Q1 2025 U.S. OOH revenue of $1.98 billion, up 2.0% year over year, with DOOH above 34% of spend and up 9.0%.

Oct. 1, 2025: FHWA transmitted FY2026 highway infrastructure program apportionments under IIJA, including $9.4544 billion of highway infrastructure program funds and $1.0 billion for NEVI formula funding.
Mar. 17, 2026: OAAA reported 2025 U.S. OOH revenue of $9.46 billion, up 3.6%, with DOOH up 10.5% and representing 36.3% of total OOH revenue.
June 24, 2026: Daktronics reported fiscal 2026 record net sales of $838.7 million, record orders of $860.8 million and year-end product backlog of $356.2 million.
June 2026: Grand View Research estimated the broader U.S. digital signage market at $7.44 billion in 2025 and $7.96 billion in 2026.

outlook.2026: The narrow U.S. variable message signage manufacturing industry is expected to reach about $7.1 billion in revenue, broadly consistent with the baseline projection, with upside from DOOH and transportation work offset by tariff and input-cost pressure.
outlook.2027_2030: Growth should remain positive but uneven as digital billboards, transportation displays and venue scoreboards expand faster than basic message centers; broader U.S. digital signage forecasts point to mid-to-high single-digit annual growth, but domestic manufacturing revenue is likely slower because hardware pricing continues to fall.
outlook.upside_case: Faster public-sector ITS deployment, continued DOOH conversion, more programmatic billboard buying, school facility upgrades and reshoring of electronics assembly would lift orders.
outlook.downside_case: A pullback in ad budgets, state DOT delays, higher tariffs, elevated metal costs or aggressive imported LED display pricing would compress revenue growth and margins.

title: Vegetable Farming in the US
one_liner: A fragmented, weather-exposed farming industry is getting a 2026 revenue lift from higher vegetable prices, while import competition, labor costs and water risk keep margins tight.
overview: The industry covers farms growing vegetables and melons in open fields and greenhouses, excluding broad-acre crops such as corn, soybeans and wheat in the baseline definition. The 2022 IBIS baseline put industry revenue at $17.623 billion after a 2017-2022 annualized decline of 5.5%, but current public USDA cash-receipts data show the broader vegetable-and-melon farm category rebounding in nominal terms: USDA ERS forecast 2026 vegetable and melon cash receipts to rise 2.7% from 2025 because of higher prices. Demand remains mature and staple-driven, but mix matters: fresh vegetables, lettuce, carrots, tomatoes and greenhouse/organic production command higher prices than many processing crops, while imports cover roughly one-third of 2025 US vegetable availability and are especially important in tomatoes and cucumbers.

key_stats.market_size: 2026F USDA vegetable and melon cash receipts: about $26.6 billion, inferred from USDA ERS forecast of a $0.7 billion increase equal to 2.7% from 2025; 2022 IBIS industry revenue baseline: $17.623 billion in 2022 dollars
key_stats.growth: 2026F USDA ERS vegetable and melon cash receipts growth: +2.7% year over year; 2026F retail fresh vegetable price growth: +6.8%; 2026F farm-level vegetable price growth: +26.7%
key_stats.profit_margin: 2022 IBIS baseline profit margin: 6.8% of revenue
key_stats.trade: 2025 USDA ERS estimated imports at about one-third of US vegetable availability; Mexico supplied about 77% and Canada about 13% of fresh vegetable imports excluding potatoes
key_stats.production: 2025 NASS vegetable and melon production was estimated for 28 crops; sweet corn and tomatoes were the largest by harvested area, and tomatoes were largest by total production

baseline_2022.profit: $1.198 billion profit in 2022, equal to a 6.8% margin
baseline_2022.exports: $3.310 billion in 2022, equal to 18.8% of revenue
baseline_2022.imports: $10.723 billion in 2022, satisfying 42.8% of domestic demand

how_it_makes_money: Farms earn revenue by selling fresh-market vegetables and melons to wholesalers, supermarkets, warehouse clubs, produce markets, foodservice distributors and direct channels, and by selling processing crops to canners, freezers, dehydrators and other food manufacturers. Pricing is set by crop quality, harvest timing, regional supply, perishability, contracts, organic certification, transportation availability and import competition. Higher-value fresh, organic and greenhouse crops support margins, while processing vegetables are more volume-driven and contract-oriented.
cost_structure: Major costs are seasonal and year-round labor, seeds and transplants, fertilizer and crop chemicals, irrigation water and power, land rent or ownership costs, machinery and depreciation, crop services, harvesting crews, packing materials, cold-chain handling, trucking and food-safety compliance. The 2026 USDA farm-sector forecast points to cash labor expenses rising 2.2% while fuel/oil and pesticide expenses decline, so vegetable growers face a mixed cost backdrop: lower some input pressure, but persistent wage, water, packing and logistics exposure.
major_players: Fragmented independent and family-owned farms: no single operator dominates the national market under the 2022 IBIS low-concentration baseline
Grimmway Farms / Cal-Organic Farms: notable large US carrot and organic vegetable grower, but still one participant in a fragmented national industry
Taylor Farms-linked grower and fresh-cut supply networks: important in leafy greens and salad channels, though much activity sits downstream from farming
Regional grower-shippers in California, Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Washington, Oregon, Michigan and Wisconsin: meaningful by crop and season rather than nationally dominant
current_dynamics: 2025-2026 conditions are price-led more than volume-led. USDA NASS reported mixed 2025 crop results: romaine lettuce value rose 46% and carrots value rose 11%, while broccoli value fell 29%, onions fell 25%, bell peppers fell 24% and spinach fell 20%. USDA ERS expects 2026 vegetable and melon receipts to increase because of higher prices, and its July 2026 Food Price Outlook shows fresh vegetables and farm-level vegetables rising faster than overall food inflation. Trade is a central issue: 2025 imports accounted for about one-third of vegetable availability, Mexico supplied most fresh imports excluding potatoes, and the 2025 termination of the Mexican tomato suspension agreement added duties that changed tomato economics for growers, importers and buyers.
whats_growing: Fresh-market lettuce, carrots, greenhouse and other protected-culture food crops, organic vegetables, direct-to-retail grower-shipper programs, and crop categories benefiting from 2026 price inflation are growing. In 2025 NASS data, romaine lettuce production rose 19% and value rose 46%, sweet potatoes production rose 31% and value rose 29%, kale production rose 134% and value rose 143%, and food crops grown under protection reached $1.01 billion in 2024 horticulture sales, up 44% from 2019.
whats_shrinking: Processing-heavy and import-exposed crops face pressure when buyers can source cheaper product abroad or when acreage and prices soften. In 2025 NASS data, broccoli production fell 18% and value fell 29%, spinach production fell 13% and value fell 20%, onions value fell 25% despite higher production, and bell pepper value fell 24%. Long-term per-capita vegetable availability is also weak: USDA ERS estimated 2024 vegetable and pulse availability at 376 pounds per person, the lowest in more than 35 years.
recent_developments: 2025-07-14: US Commerce terminated the 2019 Mexican fresh tomato suspension agreement and imposed 17.09% antidumping duties on most Mexican tomato imports.
2026-02-05: USDA ERS forecast 2026 vegetable and melon cash receipts to rise $0.7 billion, or 2.7%, from 2025 on higher prices.
2026-02-12: USDA NASS released the 2025 Vegetables Summary, covering 28 vegetable and melon crops and identifying sweet corn and tomatoes as the largest by harvested area.
2026-02-26: USDA NASS reported 2024 food crops grown under protection sales of $1.01 billion, up 44% from 2019.
2026-04-30: USDA ERS April 2026 Vegetables and Pulses Outlook reviewed tomato-market changes after the suspension-agreement shift and highlighted greenhouse crop trends.
2026-07-24: USDA ERS forecast 2026 retail fresh vegetable prices up 6.8% and farm-level vegetable prices up 26.7%.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modestly positive for revenue because pricing is doing the work: USDA ERS expects vegetable and melon cash receipts to rise 2.7% in 2026 even as broader crop receipts are nearly flat in real terms. Margin improvement is less certain because labor, water, compliance, packing and transportation costs remain structurally high, and import competition limits pricing power in several crops. The best-positioned operators are scaled grower-shippers with cold-chain access, water security, greenhouse or protected-culture capacity, organic programs and strong retail contracts. Smaller farms can still win in local, organic and specialty channels, but weather volatility, food-safety risk and buyer concentration remain material constraints.
one_sentence: Vegetable Farming in the US grows fresh-market and processing vegetables and melons for wholesalers, processors, retailers and foodservice buyers, with 2026 conditions defined by price inflation, Mexican import exposure, greenhouse expansion and uneven crop-by-crop production.

title: Vehicle Shipping Services
one_liner: Vehicle shipping services move finished cars, trucks, vans, buses, tractors and motorcycles by rail, truck and ship for automakers, wholesalers, dealers, auctions and consumers.
overview: Operators transport finished vehicles regionally and nationally, excluding towing. The 2022 baseline shows rail as the largest service line at 49.0% of 2022 revenue, local trucking at 26.0%, long-distance trucking at 22.8% and ship transport at 2.2%. In 2025 and 2026, demand is being shaped by new-vehicle sales around 16 million units, domestic assembly and tariff policy, weaker 2025 automotive trade flows, rail capacity and fuel-cost volatility.

key_stats.new_light_vehicle_sales: 16.2 million US new light vehicles sold in 2025; NADA forecast 16.0 million in 2026
key_stats.vehicle_assemblies: 10.16 million US motor vehicle assemblies at a seasonally adjusted annual rate in 2025; 9.98 million in March 2026
key_stats.diesel_cost: EIA July 2026 forecast: US on-highway diesel averages $4.61 per gallon in 2026 versus $3.66 in 2025
key_stats.profit_margin: 11.3% industry profit margin in 2022 baseline; margins remain bifurcated between high-scale rail carriers and competitive trucking operators

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from contracted or spot transport of finished vehicles, including plant-to-railhead moves, rail autorack linehaul, port-to-inland distribution, dealer deliveries, auction and wholesale transfers, consumer relocations and enclosed or expedited premium moves. Large OEMs and wholesalers usually buy capacity through contracts and logistics providers, while consumers and small dealers often use brokers or direct carrier quotes with fuel surcharges and accessorial fees.

major_costs: Labor and driver wages, especially for car-haul trucking, were a key margin pressure in the 2022 baseline.
Fuel and fuel surcharges are material; EIA forecast 2026 on-highway diesel at $4.61 per gallon versus $3.66 in 2025.
Equipment costs include tractors, trailers, autoracks, railcars, vessels, maintenance, insurance and regulatory compliance.
Purchased transportation and brokered carrier capacity are important for asset-light and overflow moves.
Depreciation and financing costs matter because car-haul trailers, autoracks and specialized equipment are capital intensive.
cost_structure.margin_pattern: The 2022 baseline margin was 11.3%; rail-linked operators tend to have stronger scale economics, while small trucking carriers face high competition, labor scarcity and fuel volatility.

current_dynamics: The market is not volume-starved in 2026, but it is mixed. NADA reported July 2026 new light-vehicle sales at a 16.3 million SAAR and kept its 2026 full-year forecast at 16.0 million units, below 2025's 16.2 million. Cox Automotive's January 2026 outlook forecast 15.8 million 2026 sales, down 2.4% from 2025. Federal Reserve data showed 2025 motor vehicle assemblies averaged 10.16 million SAAR and March 2026 assemblies were 9.98 million SAAR. Tariffs on imported vehicles and parts that took effect in 2025 shifted sourcing incentives toward US assembly, while BEV tax-credit expiration after September 30, 2025 reduced BEV share and lifted hybrid momentum in 2026. Fuel is the main cost headwind, with EIA's July 2026 outlook putting 2026 on-highway diesel at $4.61 per gallon.
whats_growing: Hybrid-related vehicle flows: NADA reported hybrid sales up 20.5% year to date through July 2026 and 15.4% of 2026 new-vehicle sales through July.
Rail and rail-connected local drayage: the 2022 baseline already had rail at 49.0% of revenue, and higher 2026 diesel costs favor fuel-efficient long-haul modes.
Domestic assembly-linked logistics: 2025 auto tariff offsets reward US production and USMCA content, increasing demand for plant, yard and dealer distribution tied to domestic output.
Digital brokerage, tracking and consumer relocation services as individual shippers demand door-to-door quotes, visibility and flexible pickup windows.
whats_shrinking: BEV-related new-vehicle volume: NADA reported BEV market share at 5.9% year to date through July 2026, down 1.9 percentage points after the federal EV credits expired in September 2025.
Import-linked ocean and port vehicle flows: BEA reported 2025 automotive vehicles, parts and engines imports down $52.0 billion, including passenger cars down $34.4 billion.
Export-linked vehicle flows: BEA reported 2025 automotive vehicles, parts and engines exports down $16.8 billion, including passenger cars down $6.9 billion.
Long-distance trucking share where rail is available, because the 2022 baseline identified rail gains and 2026 diesel costs are materially higher than 2025.
recent_developments: 2025-04: The White House modified auto and auto-parts tariff treatment, keeping 25% tariffs on many imports while adding temporary offsets for US-assembled vehicles.
2025-06: The US Department of Commerce issued procedures for auto manufacturers to apply for Section 232 tariff offsets tied to US production.
2025-09: Federal clean vehicle credits became unavailable for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, changing BEV shipment demand in late 2025 and 2026.
2025-12: NADA reported US new light-vehicle sales totaled 16.2 million units in 2025.
2026-04: Federal Reserve data showed March 2026 motor vehicle assemblies at a 9.98 million-unit SAAR versus a 10.16 million 2025 average.
2026-07: NADA reported July 2026 new light-vehicle sales at a 16.3 million SAAR and kept its 2026 forecast at 16.0 million units.
outlook: Modeled industry revenue should remain near $11.3 billion in 2026 and grow slowly through 2027, broadly consistent with the 2022 baseline forecast of about 1.2% annualized growth. Unit demand is supported by 2026 new-vehicle sales near 16.0 million, but growth is capped by high vehicle prices, auto loan rates, elevated 2026 diesel costs, weaker 2025 automotive trade and tariff uncertainty. Rail and local final-mile carriers are better positioned than long-haul truck-only operators, while brokers and large logistics platforms benefit from visibility, capacity matching and multi-mode routing.
themes: Mature cyclical demand tied to new-vehicle sales
Tariff-driven sourcing and domestic assembly shifts
EV credit expiration and hybrid growth

one_sentence: In 2026, US vehicle shipping is a mature, cyclical transport niche with roughly $11.3 billion in modeled revenue, supported by resilient light-vehicle sales but pressured by elevated fuel, financing costs, tariff-driven production shifts and uneven import/export flows.
